title: Direct identification of the child through account-bound location sharing
description: The child device sends live GPS coordinates to the backend as part of an authenticated app interaction. If the transmission is tied to an account, device identifier, or other persistent identifier, the child can be directly identified from the shared data.
assumptions: Assumes the mobile app backend can associate incoming GPS updates with a specific child account, device, or session.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context provides applicable threat types but not detailed node definitions.

title: Linkability of successive GPS updates in transit
description: Regular transmission of live GPS coordinates creates a stream of observations that can be linked together as belonging to the same child or device, revealing movement patterns and routines even if payload fields are partially pseudonymised.
assumptions: Assumes repeated updates carry stable routing, session, device, or protocol metadata, or are otherwise observable as belonging to one sender over time.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id is approximate; applicability of linkability is strong given periodic live location updates.

title: Identifiability from precise location and transmission metadata
description: Precise GPS coordinates combined with timing, network metadata, or persistent communication identifiers can make the child identifiable in transit, especially when home, school, or habitual routes are inferable.
assumptions: Assumes an observer of the flow can access payload or metadata sufficient to correlate coordinates with a real-world individual.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the identifiability risk itself is well supported by the sensitivity and precision of live location data.

title: Disclosure of highly sensitive live location data at the backend
description: The backend receives and processes continuous GPS coordinates of a child. If access controls, segregation, or downstream handling are insufficient, the destination can expose highly sensitive real-time location information to unauthorized parties or internal roles.
assumptions: Assumes the backend stores, processes, or makes the location data available beyond the minimum necessary components.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because detailed destination-side disclosure nodes were not provided in the retrieved context.

title: Unawareness of continuous child-location collection and backend use
description: Because GPS coordinates are transmitted at regular intervals, the child and/or guardian may not be fully aware of the frequency, persistence, recipients, retention, or secondary uses of the live location data once it reaches the backend.
assumptions: Assumes notices, in-app indicators, or consent flows do not clearly communicate continuous collection and backend processing practices.
uncertainty_note: Applies if transparency is incomplete; exact tree-node id is approximate.

title: Non-compliance risk from processing a child's live GPS data without adequate legal basis and safeguards
description: Receiving and processing continuous precise location data about a child may violate privacy or child-data protection requirements if the backend lacks valid consent/authorization, purpose limitation, data minimization, retention limits, or other required safeguards.
assumptions: Assumes the system is subject to privacy regulation and that child-location processing requires heightened protection.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and system context; exact tree-node id is approximate.

title: Backend stores more location data than necessary
description: The backend writes each location ping to persistent storage. If every raw ping is stored by default, the system may collect and disclose to the datastore more precise or more frequent location history than is strictly necessary for the service purpose, violating data minimization.
assumptions: Location pings contain personal data because they reveal an individual's whereabouts over time. The service may not require indefinite storage of every raw ping at full precision.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimization structure; exact subnode may differ by catalog version.

title: Stored location history enables linking of multiple events to the same individual
description: By receiving and storing each location ping, the Location History Store can accumulate records over time that are linkable to the same user, device, or account. This creates a longitudinal movement profile and enables correlation across sessions, places, and times.
assumptions: Records include a stable identifier, account reference, device identifier, or other correlatable attributes.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; threat applicability is strong if stable identifiers or consistent quasi-identifiers are stored.

title: Stored location history can identify the user
description: Location traces are often highly identifying even without explicit names, because home/work patterns and repeated visits can single out an individual. Persisting each ping in the datastore increases the chance that a person can be identified from the stored history.
assumptions: The stored pings include timestamps and sufficiently precise coordinates or place information.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; identifiability from mobility traces is context-dependent but well-established for precise longitudinal location data.

title: Location history allows inference of sensitive information
description: Once stored, repeated location pings can reveal habits, routines, relationships, and visits to sensitive places such as clinics, places of worship, political events, or workplaces. The datastore therefore enables detection of highly sensitive facts beyond the original raw coordinates.
assumptions: Historical analysis or querying of stored pings is possible, and locations can be mapped to meaningful places or patterns.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the threat clearly fits detectability/inference from stored location history.

title: Retention and secondary use of location history may exceed user expectations
description: Persistently storing every location ping may be unexpected or insufficiently transparent to users, especially if they believe location is used only transiently for immediate functionality. The datastore's receipt and retention of full history can therefore undermine user unawareness.
assumptions: Users are not clearly informed that every ping is retained, for how long, and for which downstream uses.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; this threat depends on notice/transparency actually provided elsewhere in the system.

title: Parent may disclose the child's and secondary guardian's relationship context without sufficient verification or understanding
description: By initiating an invitation for a secondary guardian to view the child's location, the parent shares personal data and relationship context (that a specific child is associated with the parent and intended co-guardian). If the parent selects the wrong recipient, is socially engineered, or is not clearly informed about what access will be granted, the act of sharing itself can disclose sensitive family and location-sharing context to an unintended person.
assumptions: The invitation contains or implies the child's identity, the parent's relationship to the child, and the fact that location access is being granted or requested.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on generic disclosure-at-source reasoning; exact sub-node may differ in the full LINDDUN Pro tree.

title: Invitation flow metadata may identify parent, child, or intended guardian
description: Even if invitation contents are protected, data in transit may expose identifying metadata such as recipient address/phone, account identifiers, device identifiers, timestamps, or tenant/family identifiers. These can identify the parent, the intended secondary guardian, or indirectly the child/family unit.
assumptions: The backend receives identifiers needed to route or process the invitation, such as email address, phone number, account id, or child/family reference.
uncertainty_note: Exact identifiers present on DF10 are not specified; threat applies if the flow carries direct or quasi-identifiers.

title: Invitation transaction can be linked to an existing family account or child profile
description: The invitation flow may carry stable identifiers or contextual metadata that allow this event to be linked with prior interactions from the same parent, child profile, household, or device. This can let observers or intermediaries correlate family-management actions over time.
assumptions: The flow includes stable account, device, session, or child/family identifiers, or repeated network metadata that supports correlation.
uncertainty_note: Applies primarily if stable identifiers or recognizable metadata are present in transit.

title: Backend may disclose location-sharing access to an unintended secondary guardian
description: At receipt, the backend processes the invitation and may create or prepare access for the invited person. If recipient binding, authorization checks, or invitation confirmation are weak, the backend could disclose the child's location-sharing capability and family relationship context to the wrong person or broader audience than intended.
assumptions: The backend stores invitation state and may trigger downstream notifications or access provisioning based on the received request.
uncertainty_note: Exact backend behavior is not described, but this is a common destination-side disclosure risk for invitation workflows.

title: Backend may process invitation and guardian data without adequate consent or legal basis management
description: The backend receives and stores personal data about the invited secondary guardian and the child's location-sharing arrangement. If it does so without recording valid consent/authorization from the appropriate parent or without supporting withdrawal and purpose limitation, the processing may be non-compliant with privacy obligations.
assumptions: The system stores invitation details and potentially personal data of the invited guardian before acceptance.
uncertainty_note: This depends on jurisdiction and product policy, but invitation workflows involving child location data commonly require strong consent and authorization controls.

title: Backend may use invitation data for secondary purposes beyond granting guardian access
description: Once received, the backend could repurpose invitation data, relationship information, or inferred family structure for analytics, profiling, growth features, or contact discovery beyond the parent's immediate intent of adding a viewer. Such secondary use would exceed the expected purpose of the flow.
assumptions: The service retains invitation and relationship metadata and has other internal uses for such data.
uncertainty_note: Potential misuse depends on system design; included because family-relationship and child-location context is particularly sensitive.

title: Backend discloses the child's live location to a secondary guardian who may not be properly authorized
description: The backend actively shares highly sensitive real-time location data with the secondary guardian. If the backend grants access without robust verification of the guardian's relationship, scope, or current authorization status, it causes disclosure of the child's location to an unintended recipient.
assumptions: Assumes secondary-guardian status can be misassigned, stale, overly broad, or insufficiently verified before sharing begins.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on generic disclosure-at-source reasoning; exact subnode may vary by the project's threat-tree version.

title: Live-location payload in transit can identify the child and associated guardian relationship
description: The data flow carries real-time location information together with account/session context needed to deliver it to the secondary guardian. In transit, these data can directly or indirectly identify the child and reveal that a specific guardian is associated with that child.
assumptions: Assumes the flow contains identifiers, tokens, or metadata sufficient to associate the location stream with a particular child or guardian account.
uncertainty_note: Exact identification subnode is approximate because the retrieved context provides applicability by threat type but not detailed tree-node mappings.

title: Repeated live-location updates enable linkability of the child's movements over time
description: Because the backend shares live location continuously or repeatedly, observations of this flow can be linked across time to build a movement history for the same child and correlate that history with the same secondary guardian recipient.
assumptions: Assumes the flow is recurring or session-based rather than a one-off coarse location disclosure.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort generic linkability node; exact subnode may differ in the authoritative LINDDUN Pro tree.

title: Secondary guardian may further disclose or expose the child's live location after receipt
description: Once the secondary guardian receives the child's live location, privacy harm can arise at the destination if they store, screenshot, forward, or otherwise expose the location beyond the intended purpose or audience.
assumptions: Assumes the recipient device or user behavior may permit onward sharing, local storage, or exposure to others.
uncertainty_note: This is a destination-side disclosure threat grounded in recipient handling; exact tree-node granularity is approximate.

title: Secondary guardian can infer sensitive behavior patterns from live location
description: By receiving live location, the secondary guardian can infer private aspects of the child's life, such as home and school addresses, routines, visits to medical or religious locations, and social patterns, beyond the minimum purpose of immediate safety monitoring.
assumptions: Assumes location precision and duration are sufficient to infer routines or sensitive places.
uncertainty_note: Exact unawareness/unawareness-related node is approximate; this is framed as the recipient learning more than the data subject may expect from the sharing.

title: Backend may share live location without valid consent or another appropriate legal basis
description: Granting a secondary guardian access to a child's live location may be non-compliant if the backend does not ensure valid parental authorization, applicable child-protection requirements, purpose limitation, and data-minimization constraints before sharing.
assumptions: Assumes the system operates in a regulated context where children's location data requires heightened protection and explicit governance.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and governance model; exact node/subnode may vary.

title: Recipient-side retention or reuse of live location may violate purpose limitation
description: After receipt, the secondary guardian may retain, reuse, or combine the child's live location data for purposes beyond the intended safety function, creating non-compliance with purpose limitation, storage limitation, or household-policy constraints.
assumptions: Assumes recipient handling is within scope of the modeled privacy analysis and that policy/legal constraints apply to downstream use.
uncertainty_note: Applicability of formal compliance duties to the external recipient may depend on system boundaries and legal role definitions.

title: Shared analytics may remain linkable to users or cohorts
description: Although described as aggregated usage and engagement analytics, the backend may share dimensions, timestamps, campaign identifiers, device/app attributes, or small-segment metrics that allow the partner to link records across reports or combine them with its own datasets, enabling linkage of user cohorts or even individuals.
assumptions: Aggregation is not guaranteed to eliminate stable identifiers, quasi-identifiers, or small-cell outputs.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context only provided applicable threat types, not detailed node mappings.

title: Aggregated analytics may still identify individuals or very small groups
description: If the backend shares granular breakdowns, rare-event statistics, location slices, or low-count segments, the partner may infer the identity of a user or a very small group from the supposedly aggregated analytics.
assumptions: Reports may include sufficiently granular dimensions or low thresholds for release.
uncertainty_note: Applies if aggregation is weak or segmentation is fine-grained; exact tree-node id is approximate.

title: Sharing engagement analytics may disclose sensitive behavior patterns
description: Usage and engagement analytics can reveal behavioral patterns such as feature use, session timing, retention, interests, or inferred preferences. Even in aggregate form, sensitive categories or stigmatizing app-use patterns may be disclosed to the partner.
assumptions: The app domain or measured events may correlate with sensitive interests or behaviors.
uncertainty_note: Disclosure risk depends strongly on app context and the granularity of the analytics shared.

title: Partner may process analytics for secondary purposes beyond funding the free tier
description: On receipt, the advertising/analytics partner may retain, enrich, profile, or reuse the analytics for its own advertising, measurement, benchmarking, or cross-client intelligence purposes beyond the original stated purpose of funding the app's free tier.
assumptions: The partner has independent commercial incentives and technical ability to combine received analytics with other datasets.
uncertainty_note: Exact downstream uses are not stated, but this is a common risk in ad-tech and analytics sharing.

title: Users may be unaware that backend analytics are shared with an external partner
description: Users may not expect that their app usage contributes to analytics shared with an external advertising/analytics partner, especially where the sharing is framed as aggregated and occurs server-side rather than through an obvious in-app action.
assumptions: The sharing is not made salient in the user interface or privacy notices.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on the transparency actually provided to users.

title: Analytics sharing may lack a valid legal basis or exceed consent expectations
description: Sharing backend-derived usage analytics with an advertising/analytics partner to monetize the free tier may require consent or another valid legal basis, purpose limitation, and appropriate contractual controls. If the sharing exceeds what users agreed to or what regulation permits, it creates non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Applicable law or platform rules treat this analytics/ad-tech sharing as regulated personal-data processing, even if data is claimed to be aggregated.
uncertainty_note: Legal applicability depends on jurisdiction, actual anonymization level, and contractual arrangements.
